blocks.text: Moreover, according to the Philosopher, History book 5, chapter 22, Αἱ δ' ἐν Θεμισκύρᾳ περὶ τὸν Θερμώδοντα ποταμὸν, ἐν τῇ γῇ, καὶ ἐν τοῖς σμήνεσι ποιοῦντες κηρία· [Hai d' en Themiskyra peri ton Thermōdonta potamon, en tē gē, kai en tois smēnesi poiountes kēria] At Themiscyra, near the river Thermodon, they make honeycombs both in the ground and in hives. And further on: Κατάγεται δὲ καὶ εἰς Ἀμισὸν ἄνωθεν μέλι λευκὸν, καὶ παχὺ σφόδρα, ὃ ποιοῦσιν αἱ μέλιτται ἄνευ κηρίων πρὸς τοῖς δένδρεσι, γίνεται δὲ τοιοῦτον καὶ ἄλλοθι ἐν τῷ Πόντῳ. [Katagetai de kai eis Amison anōthen meli leukon, kai pachy sphodra, ho poiousin hai melittai aneu kēriōn pros tois dendresi, ginetai de toiouton kai allothi en tō Pontō.] To the city of Amisus [col. 520] white and very thick honey is brought down from the higher regions, which the bees make on trees without honeycombs. Honey of this kind is also produced in other places of Pontus. Likewise: Εἰσὶ δὲ καὶ μέλιτται, αἳ ποιοῦσι τριπλᾶ κηρία ἐν τῇ γῇ· [Eisi de kai melittai, hai poiousi tripla kēria en tē gē] There are also bees which make honeycombs in a triple row on the ground ^{(5)}. Thus wild honey can be found elsewhere too; but more frequently in Judaea ^{(6)}, [III, 379] which is called more than once ^{c)} a land of oil and honey, and in about twenty places ^{d)} a land flowing with milk and honey, that is, most fertile in the produce of milk and honey. The phrase is also common among the poets: Euripides in the Bacchae, verse 142:
Ῥεῖ δὲ γάλακτι πέδον, Ῥεῖ δ’ οἴνῳ, ῥεῖ δὲ μελισσῶν Νέκταρι· — — — [Rhei de galakti pedon, Rhei d' oinō, rhei de melissōn Nektari]
The field flows with milk, it flows also with wine, it flows with the nectar of bees. Virgil, Eclogue 3:
May honey flow for him, and may the rough bramble bear amomum.
Ovid, Metamorphoses book 1, on the golden age:
Now rivers of milk, now rivers of nectar flowed.
Nectar, that is, honey, as above in Euripides. Horace, book 2, Ode 19:
— — to sing of rich streams of milk, and to tell again of honey dripping from hollow trunks.
[III, 380] Then, they say, the horses of the sun and the stars leapt in dances, and lakes of honey and rivers of milk burst forth from the ground. — — — —

Such is the mention in Iob. XX, 17 of נחלי דבש וחמאה, torrents of honey and butter. This expression is hyperbolic in such a way that it partly suits honey, because honey flows down from the comb when it is abundant. This flowing of honey is expressed in various ways among the Hebrews and Syrians. First by the word הלך halach, which properly means to go or to walk. But in 1 Sam. XIV, 26, הלך דבש is a flow of honey. So in Ovid above:
